title: Book review: Salt: A World History by Mark Kurlansky

paragraphs.text: Mark Kurlansky's Salt: A World History sets out to show that one of the most ordinary substances on any kitchen table was, for most of human history, one of the most valuable. The book moves freely across continents and centuries, from ancient China and Egypt to Roman roads, medieval Venice and the fishing ports of northern Europe. Salt was difficult to obtain in many places, and every human being needs it to live, but Kurlansky makes clear that its real importance lay elsewhere. Above all, salt mattered because it preserved food. Before canning and refrigeration, salted meat, fish and vegetables were what allowed people to survive the winter, feed armies and supply ships on long voyages.

Kurlansky is a journalist rather than an academic historian, and the book shows it, mostly to its advantage. He had already written Cod, a history of a single fish, and Salt follows a similar formula: short chapters, a constant supply of anecdotes and a willingness to follow a story wherever it leads. The result is a book that is easy to read in small portions. The cost of this approach is that the argument sometimes disappears beneath the detail, and readers looking for a clear chronological account may find the jumps between periods and places confusing. Nonetheless, the range of material is impressive, and few readers will finish a chapter without learning something surprising.

Because salt was essential, rulers were quick to see it as a source of income, and some of the book's most vivid chapters concern the resistance this provoked. Kurlansky describes the state monopolies that controlled salt in imperial China, and the French salt tax known as the gabelle, which was so widely hated that it added to the public anger that came before the Revolution of 1789. The most famous episode comes much later. Under British rule, Indians were forbidden by law to produce their own salt and were obliged to buy taxed salt instead. In 1930 Mahatma Gandhi led a march of more than 380 kilometres to the sea at Dandi, where he picked up a handful of salty mud and broke the law in front of the world's press. A tax on a cheap mineral became a symbol of a much larger injustice.

Many readers will assume that salt was always made in the simplest way, by leaving seawater in the sun until it dried. Kurlansky shows that the reality was far more inventive. Salt was cut from underground mines, boiled out of brine pumped from springs, and collected from inland lakes. In Sichuan, in western China, workers drilled wells hundreds of metres deep with bamboo tools and, remarkably, burned natural gas from the same ground to boil the brine. Some of these techniques required a level of engineering that would not be seen in Europe for centuries.

Kurlansky is at his best when he connects these large historical forces to the food people actually ate. He shows how the demand for salted cod linked fishermen in the Basque Country, Newfoundland and New England, and how salted fish travelled on to the Caribbean. He traces familiar foods such as ham, cheese, soy sauce and sauerkraut back to the need to keep food from spoiling. Less successful, in my view, are the old recipes that he places throughout the book. They are interesting on their own, but they interrupt the story at awkward moments, and I found myself skipping them in order to follow the argument.

The final chapters deal with the modern era, when salt lost much of its value. New geological knowledge revealed enormous underground deposits, industrial methods made extraction cheap, and refrigeration reduced the need to preserve food with salt at all. A substance that had once been taxed, smuggled and fought over became so cheap that it is now spread on roads in winter, and most of the salt produced in the world today is used by industry rather than eaten. Here the book could have gone further. Kurlansky mentions only briefly that many people today eat far more salt than is good for them, and a fuller discussion of the health effects of our salty diet would have made a natural ending to the story.

These are small complaints about an engaging and well-researched book. Kurlansky's central message is that the history of a single, ordinary substance can explain a great deal about how trade, politics and everyday life developed. Readers who finish Salt are unlikely to look at the salt cellar on their table in quite the same way again.

groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

items.text: According to the first paragraph, why was salt so important in the past?

options.text: It was worth more than most other goods.
It made it possible to keep food for long periods.
It was first traded along Roman roads.
It was needed in larger amounts than it is today.

items.text: In the second paragraph, the reviewer emphasises

options.text: how taxes on salt led people to resist those in power.
how governments managed to make salt cheaper.
why salt was more valuable in China than in France.
why Gandhi chose Dandi as the end of his march.

items.text: What is the reviewer doing in the third paragraph?

options.text: comparing the cost of different ways of producing salt
explaining why salt mines replaced the use of seawater
correcting a common belief about how salt was produced
describing how European engineers improved salt production

items.text: According to the reviewer, what is the central message of Kurlansky's book?

options.text: The story of a common substance can reveal how societies developed.
People today should eat much less salt.
Governments have always relied on taxing food.
Modern technology has made traditional knowledge useless.

groups.instructions: Complete the summary using the list of phrases, A–I, below.
groups.title: Salt, power and trade

options.text: producing their own salt
foreign investment
long-distance trade
state control
scientific research
reduced its value
public anger
religious ceremonies
a long walk

groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in the passage? Choose YES if the statement agrees with the views of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the views of the writer, or NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

items.text: Kurlansky is particularly good at linking historical events to everyday food.
The recipes in the book make the main argument easier to follow.
Kurlansky spent several years travelling to research the book.
The book should have said more about how salt affects people's health.

evidence.quote: Above all, salt mattered because it preserved food.

27.why: "Above all" marks the main reason: salt preserved food, so people could survive winter and supply long voyages.
27.trap: A sounds possible because salt was valuable, but the paragraph never compares it with other goods. C uses "Roman roads" from the passage, but the passage does not say trade started there.

evidence.quote: some of the book's most vivid chapters concern the resistance this provoked

pairs: led people to resist those in power
the resistance this provoked … broke the law
28.why: The paragraph is about taxes on salt and the resistance they caused: anger in France and Gandhi's march in India.

evidence.quote: Many readers will assume that salt was always made in the simplest way

pairs: the reality was far more inventive
29.why: The reviewer first states what many people believe, then shows that the reality was different. That is correcting a common belief.
29.trap: D mentions engineering, but the paragraph says Europe did not reach this level for centuries. It is not praising European engineers.

evidence.quote: the history of a single, ordinary substance can explain a great deal about how trade, politics and everyday life developed

pairs: the story of a common substance
the history of a single, ordinary substance
explain a great deal about how trade, politics and everyday life developed
30.why: The last paragraph states the central message directly, and option A paraphrases it.
30.trap: B is the reviewer's own wish from paragraph 5, not the book's message.

evidence.quote: the state monopolies that controlled salt in imperial China

31.why: A state monopoly means the government controlled salt: "state control".

evidence.quote: it added to the public anger that came before the Revolution of 1789

32.why: The passage says the gabelle added to the public anger before the Revolution.

evidence.quote: Indians were forbidden by law to produce their own salt

33.why: "Forbidden by law" means the law stopped them from producing their own salt.

evidence.quote: Mahatma Gandhi led a march of more than 380 kilometres to the sea at Dandi

pairs: a march of more than 380 kilometres
34.why: A march of 380 kilometres is a long walk, and "to the sea" matches "to the coast".

evidence.quote: the demand for salted cod linked fishermen in the Basque Country, Newfoundland and New England

pairs: linking fishing communities on both sides of the Atlantic
linked fishermen in the Basque Country, Newfoundland and New England
35.why: Salted fish connected places across the Atlantic and went on to the Caribbean. That is long-distance trade.

evidence.quote: The final chapters deal with the modern era, when salt lost much of its value.

36.why: New deposits, cheap extraction and refrigeration are the reasons salt "lost much of its value".

evidence.quote: Kurlansky is at his best when he connects these large historical forces to the food people actually ate.

pairs: linking historical events to everyday food
connects these large historical forces to the food people actually ate
37.why: "At his best" is the writer's praise, and it is about connecting history with ordinary food. The writer agrees, so YES.

evidence.quote: they interrupt the story at awkward moments, and I found myself skipping them in order to follow the argument

pairs: make the main argument easier to follow
interrupt the story … skipping them in order to follow the argument
38.why: The writer says the recipes interrupt the story and had to be skipped to follow the argument, the opposite of the statement. NO.

evidence.quote: These are small complaints about an engaging and well-researched book.

39.why: The writer calls the book "well-researched" but says nothing about how long Kurlansky spent or whether he travelled. NOT GIVEN.
39.trap: "Well-researched" makes YES tempting, but the statement adds details (several years, travelling) that the writer never mentions.

evidence.quote: a fuller discussion of the health effects of our salty diet would have made a natural ending to the story

pairs: the book could have gone further … a fuller discussion
the health effects of our salty diet
40.why: The writer says the book mentions health only briefly and wishes it had a fuller discussion. That agrees with the statement.
